data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A large service with strictly more total internal redundancy can be more resilient than a decentralized network if it can internally coordinate load-shedding and freeze dependencies on failing components, while decentralized nodes acting on identical external signals (e.g., market-based pricing) will synchronously shed load and cascade.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the decentralized network uses heterogeneous, uncorrelated monitoring signals or decision thresholds, then their failures will be truly independent and the network will be more resilient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service's internal coordination mechanism fails (e.g., the 'brain' fails), the entire system fails, making it less resilient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service shares the same external dependencies as the decentralized nodes (e.g., same cloud provider), it is not more resilient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Independently operated services that monitor the same external signals will independently arrive at the same decision (e.g., to shed load or reboot) at the same time. This algorithmic convergence acts as a hidden shared cause, creating synchronous failures that look uncorrelated but are actually perfectly coupled. A single large service, conversely, can coordinate internally to desynchronize load-shedding or isolate failing components, breaking the cascade.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
